Latest Update: Are Uranus and Neptune Secretly "Rock Giants"? A Noble Gas Might Hold the Answer

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for decades, astronomers have divided the planets in the outer solar system into two distinct camps.
  • According to recent reports, scientists are getting excited because there has been an ongoing debate that these distant worlds are actually covered in rock.
  • Industry observers note that understanding why the presence of one noble gas isotope leads to understanding whether rock is present or not requires a bit of a diversion into the world of bananas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for decades, astronomers have divided the planets in the outer solar system into two distinct camps. Jupiter and Saturn were the âgas giantsâ made up primarily of hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune were the âice giantsâ, and were much smaller but were packed with heavier elements. A upcoming paper from Olivier Mousis of the Southwest Research Institute and his co-authors, available in The Planetary Science Journal, explores whether we can use an isotope of a noble gas - argon-40 - to determine whether there are hidden mountains of rock under the ice giantâs thick atmospheres.

According to recent reports, scientists are getting excited because there has been an ongoing debate that these distant worlds are actually covered in rock. But we canât simply fly a probe out a few billion miles and drill down into their surfaces to determine that for ourselves. Instead, they decided to use proxies, such as the concentration of argon-40, as a rough measurement for how much rock there is below the atmosphere.

Industry observers note that understanding why the presence of one noble gas isotope leads to understanding whether rock is present or not requires a bit of a diversion into the world of bananas. Or at least, it gives me an excuse to talk about bananas in a planetary science article. Bananas are radioactive, and the thing causing their radioactivity is potassium-40 - a relatively unstable form of a very common element. When potassium-40 decays, it turns into argon-40, which, as a noble gas, hardly interacts with anything.

Fraser talks about how to plan a mission to Uranus.

Recent findings suggest that most of this radioactive decay takes place in rocks containing potassium-40, rather than bananas, so one of the most common sources of argon-40 is literally rocks. After it is created, it bubbles up out of those rocks and escapes into its host planetâs atmosphere. In fact, it makes up around 1% of the air youâre breathing right now.

On the ice giants, this same process could hold - argon-40 could form inside a rocky surface, and then bubble up into the planetâs atmosphere over billions of years. So we should be able to send a probe to measure the concentration of argon-40 in their atmospheres, and that would serve as an effective proxy for the existence of rock under the atmosphere.

In a recent development, thereâs just one catch - rocks arenât really the only source of argon-40. In fact, there was already plenty of it floating around in the protosolar nebula that the Sun and all the planets eventually formed out of. Therefore, Uranus and Neptune could have âtrappedâ this leftover argon-40 before they were even mature, causing argon-40 to eventually appear in their atmosphere, but not from rocky surfaces.

Fraser talks about efforts to go back to visit the ice giants of the solar system.

According to the paper, the amount of argon collected by the early versions of Neptune and Uranus depends entirely on where they formed with regards to the âargon ice lineâ. This line, which happens around 23-35 Kelvin, the temperature that argon freezes into solid ice, or is trapped inside water ice, is the determining factor of how much primordial argon Neptune and Uranus had sucked up.

Unfortunately, thereâs still a lot of debate about where exactly in the solar system the ice giants formed. If they formed close to the Sun and eventually migrated back out to the edges of the solar system, they might not have captured much argon ice, and the majority of the argon in their atmospheres would be due to release from rocks. On the other hand, if the theories about them actively moving through the solar system soon after their creation are true, then they would likely have captured a large amount of argon-40, making it useless as an indicator of whether or not the planets have a rocky surface.

Sources indicate that luckily, there is a way to potentially solve this puzzle. Argon-40 has a lighter isotopic cousin, known as argon-36, which is non-radioactive, and doesnât form in decaying rocks. Measuring its level would act like a control group, allowing scientists to estimate how much of the argon present in the atmosphere would have been swallowed at birth, as we have other estimates of the ratio between argon-40 and argon-36 in the early solar system.

Industry observers note that itâs good these sorts of insights are coming out now, as there is currently a mission, Uranus Orbiter and Probe, which is in active development and planned to arrive in the system in the 2040s. That still gives us some time to finalize our theories about what we would expect to find there. And perhaps, once it does arrive, weâll be able to definitively answer whether or not the âIce giantsâ have a truly solid surface or not.

Bourbon, lemon juice, and simple syrup make a tart, boozy drink that’s just sweet enough. It’s ideal for anyone with a minimally stocked bar and a preference for the classics.

According to recent reports, think of the Boulevardier as the Negroni’s bourbon-loving cousin. Whiskey takes the place of gin, bringing warmth and richness to the bittersweet combination of Campari and sweet vermouth. A fine choice for sipping before dinner.

A smoky mezcal cocktail with Earl Grey tea syrup and grapefruit liqueur, this bright, aromatic margarita riff is an intriguing choice for Thanksgiving brunch—or for guests who prefer tequila to bourbon at cocktail hour.

A homemade cranberry-orange jam gives this tequila cocktail a distinctly Thanksgiving twist. Lime juice keeps it tart, while a sugar-salt-and-five-spice rim adds a fragrant finish. Make the jam ahead to streamline cocktail hour.

Whether for your Thanksgiving pregame or tomorrow morning’s hair of the dog, a well-made Bloody Mary is always welcome. Worcestershire, horseradish, hot sauce, and fresh lemon give this savory classic its signature kick.

It has been revealed that A packed to-do list is no match for this make-ahead drink. Simmer red wine, cider, fruit, and spices ahead of time, then add tawny port and gently reheat when your guests arrive. Keep it warm in a slow cooker for self-service away from the kitchen.

It has been revealed that we’d welcome a pot of mulled apple cider at any fall gathering. It’s nonalcoholic, serves a crowd, and fills the kitchen with the scent of warming spices. Guests can add a tipple of brandy, bourbon, Calvados, or rum if they wish.

Can’t decide between hot cider and spice-rich chai? Have both. This cozy, nonalcoholic drink brings tea and warming spices to apple cider, making it a particularly good companion for a second slice of pie.

It has been revealed that for those who’d rather drink their Thanksgiving dessert, a warm mug of dark rum, butter, sugar, and spices delivers the goods. It’s rich, fragrant, and an excellent reason to linger at the table after the pie plates are cleared.

Blood orange, ginger, cinnamon, and cloves make this sweet-tart, nonalcoholic drink feel right at home on Thanksgiving. Prepare the shrub ahead, then top with sparkling water when guests arrive.

Who indicates a nonalcoholic spritz can’t have a little attitude? A bittersweet alcohol-free aperitif and a splash of olive brine give this savory, citrusy drink plenty of complexity. Serve it very cold, with an olive garnish.

Sources indicate that green tea, lemon juice, fresh mint, and honey make a soothing tonic after the Thanksgiving bacchanal. Alcohol-free on its own, it can take a splash of mezcal if anyone wants to steer it into cocktail territory.

It has been revealed that spiced maple syrup and cranberry juice reimagine the typical Moscow mule as a Thanksgiving drink that skips the vodka. Note that Angostura bitters contain alcohol; for a completely alcohol-free version, use an alternative like All the Bitter.

The Best Thanksgiving Side Recipes, According to Eater Editors

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.
  • The sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument.
  • It has been revealed that while we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever latest ideas have been simmering since last year’s substantial meal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.

The sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

It has been revealed that while we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever latest ideas have been simmering since last year’s substantial meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director.

I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

Nobody says they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

While more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman.

Tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest.

It has been revealed that this is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

Recent findings suggest that I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager.

Mitchell Davis, Cook and Eat Better.

Industry observers note that if I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated swiftly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be noted is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that "We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector," mentioned Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

A leading Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee introduced legislation Thursday aimed at helping regulators use technology to better spot financial stress turbocharged by artificial intelligence and around-the-clock payment systems.

Recent findings suggest that the draft bill, from Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., would require the Federal Reserve to work with other regulators to develop, test and publicly release model software that would improve the ability to assess market conditions in real time and respond rapidly to cybersecurity and other threats.

The bill is designed to help regulators keep pace with new risks "driven largely by the development of state-of-the-art AI models," according to a summary.

The legislation is intended to help regulators provide financing to banks during crises and wind down failing banks. The model software would reduce the amount of manual compliance work that smaller financial institutions would have to do by providing standard data formats for regulatory reporting and tools to manage and transmit the information to regulators, according to a Foster spokesperson.

Recent findings suggest that “With advances in AI creating latest cybersecurity threats and financial risks, it's more important than ever that we modernize the way we monitor the health of our financial institutions,” Foster remarked in a statement. “We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector.”.

In a recent development, foster, who has a Ph.D. in physics and has been a leader on AI issues on the Financial Services panel, is in line to become chair of the Financial Institutions Subcommittee next year.

He has been mulling a challenge to ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., to chair the full committee in the new Congress. But Foster is now “leaning toward not running,” a person familiar with his thinking mentioned.

Industry observers note that waters already has a confirmed challenger in Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., who on Thursday circulated a "Dear Colleague" letter seeking the support of House Democrats for his bid.

Casten touted his “career at the intersection of business, science and public policy." Before entering Congress, he worked in clean energy and co-founded a organization that converted industrial waste energy into usable power.

In a recent development, in his letter, Casten cited the need to lower housing and insurance costs, protect consumers from fraud, address risks posed by cryptocurrency and prediction markets and guard against the next financial crisis. He also promised to hold the Trump administration accountable for ethical lapses.

In a recent development, he's got a tough road ahead of him, however. Every Financial Services Democrat except Casten, Foster and Rep. Sam Liccardo of California signed an Oct. 21 letter to House Democrats in support of Waters. That show of support came after Casten made it known he was interested and it was clear that Foster had been considering his own bid.

Although Foster may not compete for the chairmanship, he has recently talked to Waters about changing how the committee operates.

In a recent development, “He wants a variety of members to play a role in legislation brought up in committee,” the source familiar with his thinking said. He’s also seeking more input on witnesses who testify at subcommittee hearings.

The draft bill he released on Thursday covers a topic that Foster is likely to pursue throughout the 120th Congress. He often asks the most questions about the use of AI in financial services at hearings and offers the most amendments related to the issue at markups.

Under the bill, model software would be developed for banking records and operations, regulatory reporting, stress testing, anti-money laundering and fraud screening, AI risk monitoring and other activities.

The software must be open source, publicly available and tested for reliability and accuracy, according to the summary. It would be tested using synthetic or legally permitted historical data rather than actual customer accounts. Regulators would not take financial or supervisory actions during the study.

The software developed during the study would not have to be adopted; rather, it “should be viewed as a starting point for further modernization,” the summary says.

All software models would have to be published within one year of enactment of the bill and a final report assessing feasibility, costs and savings, competition and other criteria, would be due to Congress within two years.

A Century-Old Pollution Disaster Has Been Discovered Frozen in Arctic Ice

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Decisions made at one Montana smelter may have shaped the air millions breathed, while Arctic ice reveals how much pollution earlier controls could have prevented.
  • More than a century ago, toxic pollution from a copper smelter in Montana was spreading across North America, reaching communities thousands of miles from its source.
  • Scientists have now used those frozen records to uncover how one industrial operation may have exposed millions of people to harmful levels of arsenic and lead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Decisions made at one Montana smelter may have shaped the air millions breathed, while Arctic ice reveals how much pollution earlier controls could have prevented.

More than a century ago, toxic pollution from a copper smelter in Montana was spreading across North America, reaching communities thousands of miles from its source. Much of that contamination went unmeasured at the time, but traces of it survived in an unexpected place: Arctic ice.

Scientists have now used those frozen records to uncover how one industrial operation may have exposed millions of people to harmful levels of arsenic and lead. The findings also demonstrate how the Earth’s ice preserves evidence of human activity long after pollution has disappeared from the air.

Sources indicate that the study, published November 10 in Nature Sustainability, was led by Joe McConnell and Nathan Chellman of the Desert Research Institute (DRI), alongside international collaborators. The team examined 10 ice cores from Greenland, northern Canada, and the Russian Arctic, finding that concentrations of toxic metals in some locations rose to approximately 15 times preindustrial levels between 1886 and 1918.

It has been revealed that the evidence pointed to the Anaconda Copper Mine complex near Butte, Montana, one of the world’s largest copper producers at the time. Researchers estimated that during its peak production decades, the operation released approximately 11,000 tons of arsenic and 4,400 tons of lead into the atmosphere each year.

“It’s pretty wild to think that a single, albeit massive source of pollution could have affected effectively the entire North American continent and western Greenland more than 4000 kilometers or 2500 miles away,” McConnell mentioned.

Using historical census records and models of atmospheric pollution, the researchers estimated that approximately 50.5 million Americans and 600,000 Canadians were exposed to arsenic concentrations associated with increased risks of lung cancer and other serious illnesses.

Sources indicate that people living near the operation faced particularly high exposure. For nearly 30 years, residents of Montana and parts of Wyoming and Idaho experienced arsenic concentrations that met or exceeded the World Health Organization’s current recommended maximum threshold for chronic exposure. The researchers also estimated that 1.4 million Americans and Canadians encountered elevated lead pollution potentially associated with cognitive effects equivalent to a 2.6-point reduction in IQ.

According to recent reports, although the study did not directly measure health outcomes, arsenic and lead exposure are associated with cancer, diabetes, cognitive decline, and heart disease. Pollution settling onto crops, soil, and water could also have created additional risks beyond those examined in the study.

It has been revealed that to reconstruct this forgotten pollution, scientists turned to the Arctic’s natural record of atmospheric change. As snow accumulates, it traps tiny particles carried by the wind, including industrial pollutants. Over time, the snow becomes ice, preserving chemical evidence of conditions from decades or even centuries earlier.

By comparing metal concentrations across the 10 ice cores, combining them with atmospheric models, and examining historical mining records, the researchers traced the contamination to northern North America. Arsenic measurements, supported by related chemical markers, closely matched Anaconda’s production history, while lead isotope evidence reinforced the connection.

Recent findings suggest that the timing also revealed how industrial decisions shaped the atmosphere. Copper demand surged during rapid electrification and the buildup to World War I, increasing pollution from ore processing. Near Anaconda, damaged crops, reduced harvests, and livestock deaths had already prompted decades of legal disputes.

Industry observers note that after the company installed pollution-control equipment around 1919, heavy-metal emissions declined by approximately 65%, according to the ice-core evidence. Similar technology had been available years earlier, but Anaconda delayed installation for roughly a decade.

The researchers calculated that installing those controls ten years sooner could have prevented another 60,000 tons of arsenic and 24,000 tons of lead from spreading across much of North America.

The Arctic record captures both sides of that history. It reveals how pollution from one industrial site reached millions of people and how changes in industrial practices eventually reduced its impact. Even today, the ice preserves evidence of environmental damage that otherwise might have remained largely hidden.

According to recent reports, reference: “Widespread North American pollution and health impacts from early twentieth century copper production” by Joseph R. McConnell, Nathan J. Chellman, Sophie M. Wensman, Alison S. Criscitiello, Andreas Plach, Dorthe Dahl-Jensen, Diedrich Fritzsche, Kira M. Holland, Drake McCrimmon, Matthew B. Osman, John Sandlos and Andreas Stohl, 10 November 2026, Nature Sustainability. DOI: 10.1038/s41893-026-01975-9.

The Simons Observatory is Online and Surveying the Cosmic Microwave Background

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1671 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the Simons Observatory in the Atacama Desert has begun its mission to survey the Cosmic Microwave Background.
  • We live in an age of large astronomical surveys, enabled by powerful computers and data handling methods.
  • There are automated surveys for transients like supernovae and asteroids, radio-sky surveys to spot objects obscured by thick dust, and massive surveys just getting started like the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's three core surveys.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Simons Observatory in the Atacama Desert has begun its mission to survey the Cosmic Microwave Background. Its goal is to detect undeniable evidence of the Significant Bang and cosmic inflation. Can this unique survey succeed where others have failed?

We live in an age of large astronomical surveys, enabled by powerful computers and data handling methods. While powerful telescopes still perform detailed observations of individual targets, and always will, wide surveys have a power all their own. The ESA's Gaia mission, for example, has completed its survey of billions of stars and generated a massive amount of foundational data that researchers will draw on for decades to come.

There are automated surveys for transients like supernovae and asteroids, radio-sky surveys to spot objects obscured by thick dust, and massive surveys just getting started like the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's three core surveys.

According to recent reports, but another Simons Observatory's survey hasn't garnered the same attention that some of the other have. The Simons Observatory (SO) consists of four telescopes working together: three small 0.5 meter aperture 'scopes in its Small Aperture Telescope (SAT) and one large 6-meter one in its Large Aperture Telescope (LAT).

The unusual configuration gives the SO the best chance to observe tiny details in the Universe's first observable light, the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB).

Recent findings suggest that this image of the Cosmic Microwave Background is from the Simons Observatory, the newest and most powerful observatory to study the CMB. It's unique arrangement of three small and one large telescope increases its resolution by an order of magnitude over its predecessor, the Planck satellite. The Simons Observatory's main goal is to find the elusive evidence from the epoch of inflation, and thereby confirming the Big Bang model of cosmology. Image Credit: Simons Observatory.

The stuff of the Universe was too opaque for light to travel through it at first. Photons were effectively scattered by the hot, dense plasma that permeated the Universe. Eventually conditions changed. The Universe expanded, the plasma cooled, and photons could travel. This was the recombination epoch and it occurred about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

Note that the name is historical and reflected our earlier understanding of the Universe. It wasn't actually a recombination, it was the first time that electrons and protons combined to form neutral hydrogen, and that's what made the cosmos transparent. Its name should probably be changed to the combination epoch.

But regardless of its name, the cosmic microwave background is the relic radiation from the Universe's first light, and it holds clues to the Universe, especially to the Massive Bang theory of cosmology.

Other efforts have been made to map the CMB. NASA's Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) and the ESA's Planck satellite both made the effort from orbit. At the moment, the South Pole Telescope (SPT) and related facilities are doing the same.

The SPT made an key discovery. It detected for the first time what's called the B-mode polarization of the CMB. The B-mode is important because it was created by primordial gravitational waves generated during the epoch of inflation, the first moments of the Universe's inflation. So finding the B-mode was important evidence for the Major Bang theory.

Recent findings suggest that the South Pole Telescope at the AmundsenâScott South Pole Station, Antarctica. The SPT is a 10-meter telescope that is credited with the first detection of the Cosmic Microwave Background's B-mode polarization. Image Credit: By Amble - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/9057466.

But there was a problem. Gravitational lensing can also create B-mode polarization, and it has nothing to do with the Massive Bang or inflation. It's difficult to tell which source created the B-mode polarization the SPT detected. So its initial detection was put in doubt.

This is where the Simons Observatory comes into the picture. It's been calibrating its instruments for two years and is now getting down to business.

âTo have all the observatory motors humming, gears turning and data flowing makes me joyful, but even more exciting is the prospect of what we could find in its massive new deep and detailed maps,â states Simons Observatory Co-Director Suzanne Staggs of Princeton University.

According to recent reports, this time-lapse shows the Simons Observatory's Large Area Telescope scanning the sky in August 2026. Credit: David Boettger.

Recent findings suggest that the observatory's four telescopes collectively have tens of thousands of microwave detectors, almost 98,000 of them. That's 16 times more than one of its predecessors, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. They're not only mapping the CMB the same way that WMAP and the Planck satellite did. They're also searching for the tiny fluctuations in the CMB, the B-mode polarizations that can confirm the Big Bang and cosmic inflation. If detected, the SO can determine if these are true artifacts of primordial gravitational waves, or artifacts of the polluting gravitational lensing that confounded the SPT.

Sources indicate that it'll take years of observations before that can be achieved, but the SO's first observations are already showing the observatory's power. Its sensitivity is meant to be an order of magnitude highter than its predecessor, the Planck satellite. âThe images that weâve made with just a few months of data are already deeper and less noisy than Planckâs, which were collected over years,â indicates Simons Observatory Spokesperson Jo Dunkley of Princeton University. That's significant, because the Planck outperformed its predecessor, WMAP, and is considered the benchmark for CMB observations. So the SO is already establishing a latest benchmark for observations.

Recent findings suggest that the SO's unique four telescope design is already showing its value. The large, 6-meter telescope is able to observe more of the sky in higher resolution than other CMB telescopes. Every couple of days, it scans half of the available sky.

âIt is incredibly satisfying to see the early maps, knowing that our initial data places us at the forefront of the field â and that we are poised to go much further,â claims Jeffrey McMahon, observatory testing lead at the University of Chicago.

The SO isn't isolated and alone in its work. All of these CMB surveys and observatories will work together in the end. For example, the SPT and other facilities at its site are mapping gravitational lenses that can interfere with the detection of B-modes from primordial gravitational waves in the epoch of inflation. Those templates can be used to help remove their pollution from CMB surveys. So it's all hands on deck.

In a recent development, this cut-away schematic indicates the Large Area Telescope's Receiver with one of its optical tubes highlighted. Note the pulse tube coolers and the dilution refrigerator. They keep the telescope at the cryogenic temperatures necessary for microwave observations. Image Credit: Simons Observatory/Nicholas Galitzki et al. 2018. Conference Proceedings.

The SO is an observer of polarized light, and that means that while its primary goal is searching for B-mode polarization, its maps have other things to reveal, too. âThere are a number of large surveys adding to our understanding of the universe,â Staggs claims. âOur idea is that we can combine our data with theirs to further our discoveries.â.

This is especially true of other wide surveys like the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time. The pair will create a potent combination for detecting transients across multiple wavelengths. âThe instrument is now sensitive enough that we can see small changes in transients in only a few days, whereas ACT took months,â Devlin says. âThis enables us to observe entirely newly introduced classes of objects.â Its science observations have barely begun, and it's already giant stellar flares and asteroids in the Milky Way, and activity around a supermassive black holes outside of our galaxy.

Industry observers note that but detecting that elusive evidence from the epoch of inflation is the SO's holy grail, and if it finds it, it will be a collective finding in the mass data the observatory will produce. Like other survey telescopes, the data will be released in large sequential data releases.

âWeâll be providing everything to the community through a data management tool, which we hope to have completed for the first data release,â Devlin says.

The initial success of its first science operations is a hopeful indication that it can finally find the evidence of cosmic inflation, the B-mode polarization from primordial gravitational waves in the CMB.

Recent findings suggest that âEssentially, right out of the box, just turning on the instrument, weâre making beautiful crisp images of the Milky Way,â Staggs states. Those images are uncovering new observations of the galaxy's magnetic fields, and understanding them is critical to understanding star formation and how the galaxy evolves.

Industry observers note that âThis moment marks a major milestone in our effort to understand these big questions about the universe,â Devlin indicates. âI think thereâs going to be so many scientific discoveries coming out in the next few years, itâll be hard to keep up.â.

The SO's performance will improve when another three small telescopes are added in 2027. That will also double the Small Area Telescope's number of individual detectors to 48,160 detectors. The original five-year survey has been extended, too.

"Combined with a planned extension of the survey duration to 2035, this expansion will significantly enhance SO's search for a B-mode signal in the polarisation of the cosmic microwave background, a potential signature of gravitational waves produced in the very early Universe," explain the authors of a 2026 paper in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.

Reconstructing Cosmic History and Earth's Evolution From Cosmic Explosions

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When we think of the Solar System, we often view it as a self-contained entity, isolated from its cosmic neighborhood.
  • According to recent reports, these include intermediate elements ranging from carbon and oxygen to iron, nickel, and radioactive isotopes thereof, as well as heavy elements like zinc, silver, tin, gold, mercury, lead, platinum, and uranium.
  • It has been revealed that the project was recently awarded a â¬3 million grant ($3.29 million USD) through the European Research Council's (ERC) Advanced Grants program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we think of the Solar System, we often view it as a self-contained entity, isolated from its cosmic neighborhood. However, scientists have long known that the planets of the Solar System are subject to activity in nearby star systems, including supernovae and other energetic astrophysical events. For example, it is established that intermediate elements and the heaviest elements on the periodic table are created when stars reach the end of their life cycle and explode, sending their outer layers (with these elements) into space.

According to recent reports, these include intermediate elements ranging from carbon and oxygen to iron, nickel, and radioactive isotopes thereof, as well as heavy elements like zinc, silver, tin, gold, mercury, lead, platinum, and uranium. At the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR), Prof. Anton Wallner and his team have released the SUPREME project to uncover traces of these elements. Their goal is to use them to reconstruct the history of cosmic events in our neighborhood and shed light on how the heaviest elements are created in nature.

It has been revealed that the project was recently awarded a â¬3 million grant ($3.29 million USD) through the European Research Council's (ERC) Advanced Grants program. Prof. Wallner and his team were one of 319 leading research groups across Europe selected for funding totaling â¬838 million ($918.86 million USD) to pursue projects that could lead to major scientific breakthroughs. The SUPREME project aims to address two fundamental questions in modern astrophysics, focusing on the past 500 million years.

Industry observers note that first, there's the question of how nearby supernovae have affected Earth and biological evolution since the Cambrian Period (ca. 538.8 to 485 million years ago), the geological era that coincided with the rapid explosion of complex marine life (aka. the Cambrian Explosion). When the Cambrian began, the continents were largely located in the southern hemisphere and were mostly barren. But as the period progressed and gave way to subsequent geological eras, life began to emerge from the oceans, giving rise to plants, mammals, dinosaurs, and eventually primates.

According to recent reports, supernovae, when they happen in our cosmic neighborhood, distribute heavy elements like gold, platinum, lead, and zinc to Earth. Credit: NASA.

Second, there's the question of how the heaviest elements in the Universe are created and distributed; in this case, to the Earth and Moon. To answer these questions, researchers at the SUPREME project will search for extremely rare radioactive isotopes in lunar samples provided by NASA, deep-sea sediments, ice cores, and other geological archives. These archives preserve the history of interstellar material that arrived on Earth over eons, allowing scientists to identify and date nearby supernovae and other nearby energetic events.

Industry observers note that their work will build on the first detection of radioactive isotopes created by a rapid neutron-capture (r-process) event in history, the process by which about half of all atoms heavier than iron are created in the Universe. This occured in June 2026, when scientists from the HZDR made the first significant measurement of curium-247 and plutonium-244 in interstellar matter trapped on Earth. As Prof. Sebastian M. Schmidt, the Scientific Director of HZDR who led the discovery team, said in an HZDR statement:.

Sources indicate that this award is a remarkable recognition of Anton Wallner's internationally leading research. SUPREME addresses fundamental questions about the origin of the elements and the history of our cosmic environment while building on measurement capabilities that are unique worldwide. We are proud that this pioneering work is being carried out at HZDR.

Industry observers note that to detect and measure rare radioactive isotopes, the researchers will use HAMSTER (Helmholtz Accelerator Mass Spectrometer Tracing Environmental Radionuclides), a new state-of-the-art accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) facility developed by Wallner and his team and installed at HZDR in 2025. Combined with an innovative laser-based technology that dramatically reduces measurement background, the team will be able to detect individual atoms with unprecedented sensitivity, opening new possibilities for astrophysics and other scientific applications.

According to recent reports, the results of this project are expected to provide unprecedented insights into the history of our cosmic neighborhood and its possible influence on Earth's geology and species evolution. "Securing one of the European Union's most competitive research grants is an outstanding accomplishment," remarked Saxony's Minister of Science, Sebastian Gemkow. "This distinction is not only a major milestone in the recipients' scientific careers, but also a significant gain for Saxony as a leading research and innovation hub.".

#65859. The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert

📅 28 Jun 2017 • ⏱️ 26m • 📚 Deep Dive (5264 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eater ↗ Open Full Page

The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert

📅 28 Jun 2017 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5264 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.
  • The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine.
  • This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.

The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

In a recent development, we update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

Newly introduced to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Industry observers note that adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he debuted Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

We update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

Industry observers note that new to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

It has been revealed that adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Open for: Lunch through late night.

As Jonathan Nunn wrote in his guide to north London’s best-value restaurants, “Durak, a tantuni salonu run by Dogan Yesil on West Green Road, is the superior late night snack template.” Only the tantuni, a speciality which originates in the city of Mersin on the southern coast of Turkey, is served here. Beef is boiled, seasoned with the likes of tomato, pul biber, sumac, and cumin and subsequently fried in cotton oil before being loaded, meat juices aplenty, inside a thin lavash with chopped parsley, tomato, and onion. It is then given a pleasing bend before being eaten; a selection of high-acid accompaniments — pickled chiles, lemon — provide the necessary cut-through.

Best for: A snack on the way home after a long day.

According to recent reports, mukaddes Yadikar’s restaurant near Walthamstow Central station opened in London in summer 2017. It was London’s first strictly Uyghur restaurant, and has become perhaps E17’s finest neighborhood restaurant. To start, go for the Chaomian, a stir-fry of short noodle snippets wokked with chunks of beef, spring onion, and tomato. Third, and most importantly, get the signature da pan ji (“substantial plate chicken”): a remarkably deep, savoury, and spicy chicken and potato stew, teeming with Sichuan peppercorns, served with flat hand-pulled noodles. This is a warm, homely, and treasured space to eat in east London.

Best for: Casual dinner with a group.

Open for: Lunch and dinner on weekends, dinner only during the week.

Eater London’s Restaurant of the Year 2022 comprises three discrete yet intertwined endeavors. Downstairs in the basement kitchen, George Jephson butchers whole animals, repurposing them as immaculate charcuterie, while upstairs, chef Mike Murphy uses excellent ingredients to prepare simple plates that lean French and southern European — think trout poached in butter with roe and sorrel; or a roast game bird with quince and bitter leaves. Sommeliers Tom Beattie and Fran Roberts, the duo behind the wine importer bearing both names, run the bar and the floor with a small team. Cadet is a wine bar, a restaurant, a charcutier, and a shopfront; it feels French and it feels London; and, from the moment it opened, it has always felt just right.

This diminutive Vietnamese shop on Hackney’s Graham Road serves one of the city’s best sandwiches — inside one of the city’s best baguettes. Although the spot has just one table and three or four seats, it’s difficult to think of warmer hospitality than at Bánh Mì Hội-An. The duo behind the counter prepare fresh sandwiches to go, and while the pork classic is excellent, don’t sleep on the turmeric-heavy fried catfish on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays; fragrant with coriander, mayo, fermented chile paste, sriracha, and pickled vegetables, it is an object lesson in flavor, texture, and balance.

Ex-Noma sommelier Yukiyasu Kaneko’s wine bar, set in a cozy space beneath a railway arch close to London Fields, may yet become the new template for natural wine bars, a category that has grown a little tired and derivative. Few other businesses can rival Yuki’s assured sense of self and pleasing ambience. An extensive (and fairly priced) list includes highlights from the Jura, Savoie, and Loire regions, as well as bottles from elsewhere in the Old World. Food is secondary but not an afterthought, with snacky dishes such as eggs with tahini, house-made potato crisps dressed with sansho pepper, cured beet tops, silken tofu with mushrooms, and made-to-order beef tartare.

Must-try dish: Ask Yuki for his best wines from the Jura or the Savoie.

Industry observers note that these days, London has no shortage of excellent new-age wine bars. It’s been a signature category in the city since the days of P. Franco and the likes of Terroirs before. But in more recent times, spots like Cadet, Hector’s, and Yuki Bar have raised the standard of wine bars sharply. At Goodbye Horses, which opened in the second part of 2024 (and where I enjoyed one of my favorite nights out last year), sommelier Nathalie Nelles oversees one of the most interesting wine lists in the city. Nelles has a penchant for excellent French wines from the Jura, Loire, and Burgundy. Go in the evening to enjoy a selection of small plates, which might include an avant-garde beef tartare, some carefully arranged crostini-like toasts, and a cheese plate. But you’re here to drink, really, and to take in the quite extraordinary interior, hand-painted curtains and long, organically shaped wooden bar — which lend the room a World of Interiors vibe in the best way.

Must-try: Complex savagnins from the Jura, elegant chenin blancs from the Loire Valley, grower Champagnes, and a mix of modern and classic wines from regal Burgundian producers.

East Ham is home to London’s largest Kerala community and its greatest concentration of South Indian restaurants. The pick of them is Thattukada, run by chef-owners Biju and Preeti Gopinath. Curries and roasts have a depth of flavor and spicing that belie their simple descriptions, and they should be mopped up with crisp parottas or snow-white appams. But it’s the legendary fries that are unmissable: half a chicken cut into segments, then aggressively and skillfully fried with chiles and crispy onions; little netholi (anchovies) cooked and eaten whole; or battered mussels that pop thrillingly in the mouth.

Must-try dish: Get the mussel fry.

This elegantly designed wine club beneath a Haggerston railway arch now firmly belongs in the top bracket of (French) restaurants in London. Chef Seb Myers and his modern-ish, playful take on French country cooking fits perfectly with the fascinating and broad wine list owned by patron Jonathan Alphandery. With dishes such as a red mullet tartine; grilled leeks vinaigrette with Tunworth cheese; a duck offal choux farcis; and mackerel with coco beans and greens; as well as a caramel tart with blue cheese, Planque has nearly everything that makes a great modern European restaurant great.

Best for: Pairing some of London’s cleverest cooking with some of the best wine in the city.

Open for: Lunch and dinner, with brunch on weekends.

Since Cafe Cecilia opened in 2021, it has maintained a steady flow of plaudits from all the coolest places, in part because of chef-owner Max Rocha’s connection to the world of fashion (father John and sister Simone are designers). However, there’s a surfeit of substance as well as style in this stark, minimalist cafe-bistro. And playfulness, too, seen in the likes of recreations of chicken Kievs or deep-fried bread-and-butter pudding in a pool of cold custard. Rocha and his staff are direct descendaents of the ingredients-obsessed tradition of St. John, the River Cafe, and Quo Vadis. Like peer Anna Tobias’s cooking at Cafe Deco, Rocha’s can be colored a bit beige, but it deserves the attention it has received.

Must-try dish: Do not miss the steak and chips with peppercorn sauce, nor fruit tart at dessert.

In a recent development, this quaint place close to King’s Cross hasn’t been open long, but has been a conversation starter the likes of which the London restaurant scene hasn’t seen for years. Chef and Belfastman Hugh Corcoran’s sub-20-seater venue is open only at lunchtime (midday and 2 p.m. sittings are offered), reservations must be made via the restaurant’s landline (or postcard, honestly), it is cash-only, and the wine menu is all kept inside the faintly grumpy, periodically affable proprietor’s head. You can skip the starters (save, perhaps, the homemade soda bread and butter); just head straight to the mains, where you might find a slice of game bird pie with mash, a portion of braised guinea fowl with cabbage, or a fantastic rendition of a Dublin classic — coddle: boiled, peppery white sausages in a salty broth with root vegetables and lots of allium. This place eschews everything that the London restaurant industry has become, while bringing forth some (if not all) of the good things it once offered. And you can say, “I was there then.”.

In a recent development, the area around Euston station is replete with no-frills, delicious places to eat. This little Malaysian basement setup from chef Sugen Gopal on Doric Way may be the best. Two pieces of freshly made, high-moisture roti canai — to eat in or take away — are best served with curry dal. Roti King has a few other locations throughout London as well.

Know before you go: The new online queueing system makes for a seamless experience.

Chef Ed Wilson’s hearty French Italian menu is a showcase for his own personal love of food. To eat here is to share that passion, especially now with an increased emphasis on fresh pasta and spectacular comfort food. Wines are predominantly natural and biodynamic. Illustrated wine posters, art, and curios on whitewashed brick walls also make the two relaxed dining rooms on Columbia Road among London’s most handsome and cool.

Vibe check: This place has the city’s smallest and most beautiful bathrooms — among the very first to use Aesop, too.

Recent findings suggest that at the late chef Kate Armah’s outstanding neighborhood Ghanaian restaurant in east London, the sharing platter — which includes tsofi, chicken wings, kebabs, plantains, and more — might be the definition of generosity in hospitality. Other highlights here include akonfem (guinea fowl), red red (fried plantain with black eye bean stew and gari foto), and any of the soups, which come served with choice of starchy sides such as fufu, kenkey, kokonte, or rice.

Vibe check: As the venue of choice for many visiting musicians and performers, Kate’s might be London’s least-appreciated celebrity restaurant.

There is no shortage of decent pizza in this town, but reliably excellent Latest York-style slices are harder to come by. Tom Vincent’s Vincenzo’s, which has been a bona fide IYKYK destination in Bushey, Watford for the last half decade, made its arrival in central London at the end of 2025 and since then has been treating the city to an excellent roster of classics and innovative pies. There are cheese, tomato, and pepperoni pizzas, all featuring low-moisture mozzarella, good tomato sauce, and a delightfully crisp base. U.S. colleagues might even admire the resistance to tip dip. Beyond the classics, look out for a spanakopita slice featuring feta, creamed spinach, and a Scotch bonnet honey; and the lesser-seen, thicker-based grandma pie for the heads, sometimes topped with vodka sauce, other times with pepperoni and hot honey.

Best for: Probably the best pizza slice in town.

After a refurbishment of both kitchen and premises, this haven on Farringdon Road is back to the form that has made it one of the most essential of the city’s essential kitchens in recent years. Chef Nick Bramham’s cooking now leans more towards the Aegean, with the likes of giouvarlakia bringing herbed meatballs bobbing in avgolemono. The menu will change weekly and will travel across southern Europe, but look out for Bramham’s clever riffs on BLTs, lobster rolls, and perfectly seasoned pasta dishes, after peerless gildas, before flawless sour cherry cannoli.

Must-try dish: When Nick does pasta or Nick does a sandwich, you must order it.

Industry observers note that clerkenwell’s Sushi Tetsu might be the hardest reservation in London. It also pound-for-pound serves the best (value) sushi in the city. To observe Toru Takahashi’s knife skills and to eat his omakase menu while receiving Harumi Takahashi’s gently flawless hospitality (the two are married) is to experience one of London’s most complete and completely brilliant restaurants.

Know before you go: There are only seven seats in the restaurant, all at the sushi counter.

While the original St. John is rightly regarded as the most important British restaurant in a generation, Bread and Wine, the sibling site in Spitalfields, is a better and more interesting restaurant today. If food were a religion, then this would be its church. Welsh rarebit, bone marrow and parsley salad, foie gras on toast, mussels with cider, deviled kidneys, half a dozen madeleines, and a whole pie, which might be filled with pheasant, bacon, and trotter. Praise be.

Best for: Lunch is one of the purest, most heavenly restaurant experiences in London.

Joké Bakare’s small, two-story central London venue is no secret to anyone interested in restaurants: The chef’s modern recreations of classic dishes from Nigeria and the broader West African region have earned recognition from across the globe, including from the Michelin guide, which awarded Chishuru a star. As well as the chef’s immense presence, inventiveness, and ability to convey her love of food, the brilliance of Chishuru’s menu is rooted in age-old practices of fermentation, which lend many of the dishes a deep and lasting umami. It’s there in dishes like beef sirloin and dawadawa short rib with Tokyo turnip and a bitter leaf sauce, as well as grilled guinea fowl breast with celeriac cake, jalapeño, and egusi sauce.

Must-try dishes: Be sure to try Bakare’s jollof rice, and leave room for dessert.

Given the pace at which restaurants are modernizing and as the internationality of food becomes ever more commonplace, the Ledbury’s tablecloths and Franco-modern European style might be classified as old-school-ish. But that would be to ignore the level of craft and conscientious sourcing, and its application of Japanese ingredients and techniques in dishes like Cornish bluefin otoro with miyagawa and black sesame; or veal sweetbread with parsnip, liquorice, pear, and sansho pepper. And, finally, to consider the Ledbury a relic would be to overlook the profound influence chef-owner Brett Graham has had on the professional development of many of London’s best modern chefs — from BRAT to the Clove Club and beyond.

Best for: Birthdays, anniversaries, and one of the most special fine-dining experiences in the city.

Chef Meedu Saad’s hotly-anticipated Soho restaurant feels all at once brand new, a fixture of Soho and primed to remain in situ for years to come. Super 8, the group behind it and celebrated venues like Kiln, Brat, and Mountain, has a knack for creating the restaurants that Londoners (and tourists) really want, before they know they want it. Impala embodies the qualities that give the group its edge — a buzzy, handsome dining room, thoughtfully curated playlists, attentive and cool service, plus clever dishes prepared with fine, carefully-sourced produce. The group also promotes its best talent to give them a platform; in Saad, backed by development chef Songsoo Kim, they have a star. This north Londoner, British Egyptian chef is cooking his own food: North African leaning with French and modern British accents, most of it over hot coals or from a wood-fired oven. Try the aish balady with Tunisian harissa, ftira with egg, a grilled squid and green leaf salad, sheftalia, molokhia with lamb, Cantonese-ish-style roast duck with fig sauce, or an elegant pilaf. And save room for the one dessert: a pistachio and date custard tart.

Sources indicate that must-try dish: Cantonese-style roast duck with molasses and fig sauce. (Get it with the pilaf.).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

Shuko Oda’s little bar in Soho is among London’s most acclaimed Japanese restaurants. Over a long, blond wooden counter, chefs calmly and politely pass hot bowls of steaming broth containing noodles made on-site, topped with proteins like tempura prawn or smoked mackerel, or seasonal green vegetables from Sussex farm Namayasai. The traditional Japanese breakfast is the most steadying in London.

Know before you go: The specials board of small plates changes every day and exhibits some of the city’s best modern British cooking.

In a recent development, bar Italia remains one of London’s most precious institutions, a relic of the mid-20th century sitting indomitably on Soho’s Frith Street. More than almost anywhere else in the capital, Soho is a victim of change, fads, and nonsensical restaurants. (True story: A half decade ago this same street played host to a venue called Flavour Bastard.) But Bar Italia never changes. And for that, we must be grateful. Its consistency and sense of self is what makes it so steadying and reassuring in a world of flux and uncertainty. At Bar Italia you always know your espresso will be bitter, your Peroni will be cold, and your bacon ciabatta will be better than almost anything else you can get in this storied but spoiled patch of the city.

Best for: An iconic, reliable breakfast and espresso.

For my money, Ikoyi may be the choicest special occasion venue in the city. Chef Jeremy Chan and restaurateur Iré Hasan-Odukale’s venue has evolved since its inception in St. James’s in 2017. It now occupies a sleek location in the bowels of 180 The Strand and has matured accordingly, elevating the food yet further to match its fancy new surroundings. While it is still philosophically rooted in the culinary traditions and flavor profiles of Nigeria and the West African region, Ikoyi is now an archetype of the Ultra-Modern European genre. Recent meals have featured the seductive savory deliciousness of Chan’s signature smoked jollof rice, and the precise application of spice and chile heat to immaculately cooked protein will blow you away, whether it’s sweetbread suya, dry-aged turbot, or charcoal-grilled lobster. A special restaurant, deserving of its two Michelin-starred status.

Best for: A true blowout dinner.

Recent findings suggest that gerrard Street’s Cantonese institution needs little introduction. Wong Kei is a decades-old London restaurant famous for its multistory dining room, roast meats (duck, char siu), wontons, red-ringed plates, and the now-cult (if much overstated) brusque service. Its enduring appeal — in spite of newer, trendier, regionally diverse restaurants in central London’s Chinatown — is its faithfulness to the traditions of dependable and delicious Cantonese cooking in the U.K., the stuff of a bygone era. In other words, it’s a giant, 500-seat living monument to a time before bubble waffles and Instagram-first openings.

Best for: A nostalgic UK-Cantonese meal with a group.

Chef Normah Abd Hamid and her family team offer a Malaysian comfort menu that makes the restaurant one of the best in the city from a nook of a unit in Queensway Market. Sour, hot assam pedas; roti to rival London’s King in Euston; and beef rendang or nasi lemak to go alongside. Normah’s is quaint and Normah is brilliant; this remains one of central London’s best restaurants to visit with a small group of friends and one to take out-of-towners visiting the city.

Know before you go: The food is halal, and no alcohol is allowed on site.

Sources indicate that mayfair’s two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of a few places in London that manages to straddle the line between celebrity hype and quality cooking. Tandoori masala lamb chops, chicken butter masala, and the trademark wild muntjac biryani remain standouts 13 years after it arrived on Albemarle Street. The prices match the level of cooking and the illustrious surroundings, making this one for special occasions.

Best for: Special occasions, atmosphere, and some of the finest curries in the city.

Together with Saikei, this is one of the great places in London to eat dim sum — particularly, with a big group on a Sunday lunchtime for the whole experience, driving out to the Docklands, walking up the wooden staircase to above a mixed martial arts gym, and putting your name down among the dozens of others to wait for a table. Once inside and seated, it’s a procession of tea and food. Be sure to order extra of the prawn and chive dumplings, and the special fried cheung fun with XO sauce (one of the best rice noodle dishes in the city). You might plump for sui mai, tripe, or some ribs. Barely anything you choose will disappoint. And from there, it might be a selection of sticky-sweet roast meats, or a Cantonese-style steamed seabass with ginger and spring onions and rice to share for the table. There is no way you’ll leave unsatisfied; lunch at Yi-Ban is pure nourishment.

Best for: Sunday lunch with a group (and plane spotting at City Airport).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

It has been revealed that there’s something lazily obvious about including the Ritz on a list of essential restaurants in London, but credit where credit’s due. The chef in charge comes fully garlanded: John Williams MBE is the master of niche, old-school French fine dining, delivering dishes of exceptional precision, yet never at the expense of deliciousness. Despite much frippery and eye-watering expense, when you get down to the brass tacks of a meal at the Ritz, it’s really quite simple: immaculately seasoned ingredients, assembled into balanced dishes, cooked adroitly. That’s true across the menu, but nowhere more so than in the Dorset crab with creme fraiche and Imperial caviar; filet of veal with white asparagus and lovage; the classic beef Wellington; and the theatrical crepe suzette.

Know before you go: The restaurant will make sure you comply with the formal dress code.

It has been revealed that A treasure. Unmoved by the comings and goings of trends, Bermondsey’s 40 Maltby St is a 40-cover answer to the question, pejorative as it may often be: What is British food? Steve Williams is a chef’s chef, cited by James Lowe, Brett Graham, and Florence Knight in their top five in the city. Raef Hodgson of distributor Gergovie Wines — which features low-intervention styles — runs the front-of-house without hubris. Recent dishes included winners such as pork schnitzel with raw celeriac, mustard, and braised potatoes, onion, and thyme, or a chestnut and brown sugar meringue.

Know before you go: Check Instagram for the menu, which always features an in-joke or two.

In a recent development, this vast restaurant dining room sits quite inexplicably on the ground floor of a Holiday Inn Express budget hotel just off the A102 on the south exit of the Blackwall Tunnel. But this is a destination dining room of tremendous pedigree. A mid-length, high-quality dim sum menu features a must-try fried prawn and Chinese chive number that stakes a fair claim to being the best single-bite hot item in the city — a crispy, fatty, sweet, salty umami nugget. Among the noodle plates to share, king prawns are excellent, with the noodles taking on the requisite smoke from the wok, seasoned judiciously. Saikei is a close-to-perfect family and group dining experience.

Best for: Sunday lunch, preferably with a large group.

Open for: Dinner to late night during the week, lunch to late night on weekends.

Industry observers note that in his guide to the city’s best East African restaurants, Riaz Phillips says Adulis’s “palatial setting has to make it one of the finest east African and Eritrean restaurants in the capital.” The dark wooden fixtures give every meal here a sense of occasion. The restaurant is well-suited to solo or group dining, with a menu offering selections for one, two, four, and eight persons. Look out for kwanta fitfit, smoked, dried beef with green chile and injera; zilzl assa, grilled red snapper seasoned with Eritrean herbs; and the entire range of vegetarian and vegan stews, comprising spinach, beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all eaten with more of the excellent, subtly tangy, and moreish injera.

Best for: A special occasion with vegetarians and vegans.

Open for: Dinner on weeknights, brunch through dinner on weekends.

The second branch for this south London institution, Nandine — “kitchen” in Kurdish — is run by Pary Baban, husband Pola, and sons Rang and Raman. During the day it serves a menu of brunch dishes, meze, and intricate pastries. Technicolored and abundant meze platters served in the evening include kubba (minced beef and rice patties), onion dolma, and qawarma. Pastries like borek, made with a Kurdish pastry called galgali, and baklava are not to be missed.

Best for: Go for brunch and get the meze, for yourself.

Bruce Poole’s Wandsworth Common institution is best summed up thus: technique, decadence, and salt. There’s skill and execution here that no longer feels commonplace in restaurants in London (explained, perhaps in part, by how out-of-London it feels). It’s classical in almost every sense; the dining room has the breezy, impressionist art-covered air of a destination neighborhood bistro in which Michelin’s inspectors would feel welcome. But what it lacks in newly introduced-wave imagination over the course of a meal, it makes up for in professionalism and elan. My favorite dish during a recent visit was a “homemade” (you’ve gotta shout about these things in buzzy Wandsworth) cavatelli with duck and morteau sausage ragu, showered with Parmesan: rich, moreish, sumptuous — a flawless small plate of pasta.

Best for: Special occasions, especially including a glass or two of vintage Champagne.

Possibly London’s best Jamaican jerk shop. On the edge of Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park, with a smoky aroma detectable from many hundred meters, this stark room is dedicated to one thing: immaculately, judiciously seasoned protein grilled without remorse. The age of these oil drums and the time-honored expertise of chef Murphy Lawrence and his team result in jerked pork belly, chicken, goat, and even lobster, all penetrated with smoke and lifted by allspice, Scotch bonnet, and salt. Tasty Jerk is a heady, intoxicating, and remarkably good-value eating experience.

Know before you go: Buy a bottle of the home-made pepper sauce to take away, but use with caution and keep it in the fridge.

Fascinated by British meats and Thai cooking preparations, restaurateur Ben Chapman opened this homage to northern Thailand on Brewer Street in Soho 10 years ago this year. It has always been a dynamic showcase for rare-breed British meat in spicy, piquant laabs, Cornish dayboat fish in bright seafood curries, and complex, herbaceous salads (a mix of British leaves and Thai herbs), the like of which are seldom found anywhere in the capital. Almost all of the cooking here is done not with electricity or gas, but over charcoal.

Must-try dish: Claypot glass noodles. Don’t skip the wine list.

Recent findings suggest that despite the proximity of France to Britain, the restaurant traditions and contemporary scenes have little in common. There is just something – the je ne sais quoi – about bistros in France which isn’t often found in venues on this side of the channel. But there are those who manage to recreate the mythos and romanticism of the bistro-proper. Chef Henry Harris’s longstanding practice in the field of French cooking lends him a rare level of expertise. His Bouchon Racine sits above a pub close to Farringdon station, and it feels like a bistro – tables are close, there’s little in the way of frippery, the menu is written out in chalk on a blackboard, which is moved around the dining room. It’s difficult to choose, but a good place to start is with a plate of paté or terrine, followed by one of the finest versions of rabbit in mustard sauce; confit de canard; or a côte de boeuf to share. It would be rude not to finish with a crème caramel and a pate of cheese.

Best for: Lapin à la moutarde, French bistro classics.

Open for: Lunch and dinner during the week (but check opening hours; reservations by email only.).

Best for: The most delicious, hyper-seasonal cooking in the city right now.
